summary:
Dancing with the SARs is a web platform that turns NISAR radar data into change maps anyone can read. Users pick a site and two dates, and the platform shows a before/after comparison of L-band GCOV backscatter. The data is radiometrically corrected, aligned and converted to dB, with change thresholds at 2, 3 and 6 dB. Results are pre-computed, so there is nothing to install or run, and each one can be exported as a GeoTIFF, web tiles and a manifest recording its dates, thresholds and statistics.

NISAR data is massive and hard to process, which keeps its insights out of reach of the people who need them. Our platform removes that barrier. It ingests NISAR GCOV products and presents surface change through an interactive map, with no SAR expertise required. We demonstrate it on two 2026 events: the Anak Krakatau eruption, which added 32.8 hectares to the island, and the Trishuli flood in Nepal.

This matters because radar sees through clouds and darkness, exactly when disasters strike. Making its evidence clear and traceable helps decision-makers respond faster.
details:
Dancing with the SARs is a web platform that turns NISAR radar data into change maps anyone can read. NISAR is the NASA-ISRO L-band SAR satellite. A user picks a site and two dates. The platform reads the NISAR L2 GCOV backscatter products for that site, applies radiometric correction, aligns and smooths the two images, and converts them to dB. It then shows a before/after comparison with change thresholds at 2, 3 and 6 dB. Everything is pre-computed. The user opens the site and explores the results, with nothing to install, no processing to run and no database to manage. Each result can be exported as a GeoTIFF for analysis, as 256 px PNG tiles for the web, and as a manifest listing the dates, thresholds and statistics.

We demonstrate it on two events from 2026. At Anak Krakatau, the early-September eruptions added 32.8 hectares to the island, visible in the 13 August vs 30 September NISAR backscatter. At Trishuli in Nepal, a Himalayan avalanche on 26 August caused a flood with roughly 10 minutes of notice, which shows the need for a more comprehensive monitoring system.

We want surface changes caused by disasters, such as eruptions, floods and landslides, to be communicated quickly and clearly to decision-makers, not only to radar specialists. Faster, more legible evidence supports emergency response and long-term monitoring. The same pipeline can be pointed at new sites and new NISAR acquisitions, and it can fetch new observations live from ASF/Earthdata.

What our team considered

  • Audience: decision-makers and the public, not SAR specialists.
  • Honesty about the data: we show the processing identity and the provisional status of the products, we state that the builder does not resample the data, and we keep thresholds fixed and visible instead of presenting a single unexplained score.
  • Reproducibility: acquisition IDs, dates and parameters are recorded in the manifest.
  • Scale: NISAR volumes are very large, so we pre-compute and tile results to keep the site fast.
  • Real events: we chose two contrasting, recent disasters (a volcanic eruption and a glacial flood) to show the approach is not tied to one hazard.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Data: NISAR L-band GCOV (HH and HV) from ASF/Earthdata, 10 m grid, EPSG:32748, provisional product status.
  • Backend: FastAPI serving the pre-computed files.
  • Frontend: Next.js with a Mapbox map and a before/after reveal slider.
  • Outputs: GeoTIFF, PNG tiles and a JSON manifest.
